Warhammer, Dawn of War 2 is a really great fundamental RTS game for learning micro.

Micro vs. Macro

In RTS games where you build an economy, and where you have allies you need to keep track of, and where there are objectives to capture/destroy, that is the "Macro". Some players excel at "the big picture".

In modern RTS games and MOBAs, "Micro" plays a larger and larger role. Some games try to balance the Micro and Macro, some games pretty much ignore one in favor of the other, and some games just spend more time focusing on the visceral experience. In MOBAs such as DOTA, the micro game includes "Last-Hits" which completely change the character level progression and can decide games.

  • Take a way 1 - Effective Micromanagement is focused on the right things

The visceral experience in Dawn of War 2 is just distracting. Mostly it is not helpful. Watching the pretty carnage of battle is an easy way to end up losing a unit to something you didn't notice. So an example in Dawn of War 2 is that effective micromanagement is focused on the right things. You can see health bars on the character portraits, you can see energy levels. On the battlefield you can see if the soldier is suppressed or engaging efficiently. I spent the first few characters spending so much time watching the wonderful carnage that I was not effective.

  • Take a way 2 - Sometimes you can be too specialized

The first 4 starts I overspecialized. My commander character can don a Power Fist and just wade through the game, but to make any real progress in the campaign you need balance. By around day 30 in the campaign, I hadn't given several of my squads any hand to hand ability and they began being picked off between waypoints by small ambusher units. Sure they could wield flamethrowers, which are super fun, but any time the lines were swamped they just got dead. Sometimes you can be too specialized - and it is helpful to think of a game from a game design perspective and utilize the 'Health' and 'Melee' stats to round out your characters, since the game included them - even if you don't consider your scouts to be useful in hand to hand. It turns out they aren't deadly with hand to hand, but they can defend themselves for long enough to be rescued by an assault marine with only a few points in Melee.

  • Take away 3 - Lower Difficulty allows flexibility

I play on "Hard" which generally forces me to learn more nuances in a game engine than if I played on "Story" or "Normal". On "Normal" you could just give all your points to get that Power Sword for your commander, all the shooty things for your Heavy Gunner, and make your Scouts into merciless silent Sniper Assasins. Lower Difficulty allows flexibility which isn't available on harder levels. On harder levels, you must reign in your desire to create the most DPS & Burst DPS to allow for survivability and adaptability.

  • Take away 4 - Keyboard Shortcuts

So by Character Level 10 in Dawn of War 2 you will have 4 squads. You can arrange them in any order, and they can be numbered 1,2,3,4 and selectable on your keyboard. But in boss battles, sometimes you might need to move 2 squads quickly. Other times you might have 2 squads that are filling a similar role, or a complementary role. [Such as if you group your Shotgun Scouts with your Melee-Front line scrappers they make an excellent grouping]. So for example in this game, the options screen alluded to the fact that the groups can be re-numbered and stacked. So if you want "Tarkus" and "Cyrus" to be available by pressing #2 on the keyboard, you can do so. [Then hit "Tab" to subselect within that group].

Fundamental things like this, which create habits which are used by default, become exponentially rewarding over time.

  • Take away 5 - What the Game Designers are trying to tell you

In this game there is a pretty stark contrast between the "regular" missions and the "defense missions". Namely, it is intended that you fail at many of the "regular" missions. The game design has built in reinforcement of the idea that failing a mission is OK, such as the fact that many maps have 2 'optional' objectives and you need to play the map twice to get them both. But surely you're not meant to fail every mission - and that is where 'defense missions' come in. Lessons 2 & 3 prove this out; upon first attempts characters which were too specialized were useless in the 1-shot-only defense missions.

https://i.pinimg.com/originals/87/69/66/8769663ec297e241f4afa87f9d9c73c9.jpg
The lessons of failure - Space Marine Style

Concerning Takeaway 1: The entire micro-clickfest you see in many modern RTS game imho largely stems from the fact that they're designed to pick up the MOBA/Esports fad. Which means that, when in doubt, the designers may make the game very fun and/or spectacular to watch, but less entertaining to play because only elite players can juggle six or eight different squads of units, all with their respective special abilities. That you constantly have to babysit them all the time because a fully wiped squad loses all those sweet EXP it accumulated only adds to that.

Concerning Takeaway 2: I really remember that differently, in that most squads were fairly tied down to one specific tree while the two other options were nice-to-have thingies if you had maxed out the first tree. I.e., Thaddeus could be skilled range-centric so his Beakies could equip flamers or stuff, but then again, the entire point of assault marines is to jump into the thick of enemy ranged specialists and fuck their shit up in melee. Same with Avitus and his (limited) melee abilities while devastators are there for ranged firepower, etc. I will say, however, that I was disappointed over the Force Commander and Davian Thule being more or less actively pushed into the melee corner because you needed someone to tank those carnifexes and other heavy-melee units, something for which Thaddeus was just to brittle.

Takeaway Five: Defensive missions imho were intended to be harder than (most) regular missions because they were bonus missions in themselves, awarded to you if you finished regular missions with as much kills as possible, etc. Needless to say, they still were not entirely optional unless you wanted a non-standard gameover by having the Nids tentacle-rape the entire sector.
